newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian firms nibble on bullet of cutting jobs.
newsitem.headline: Russian firms nibble on bullet of cutting jobs.

text.p: Two of Russia's biggest firms plan to shed thousands of jobs, but analysts said on Friday that the cuts were a tiny fraction of those needed for the industrial giants to compete with the outside world.

Natural gas monopoly producer Gazprom and metals mining concern Norilsk Nickel said this week they were cutting their bloated workforces. Analysts welcomed the move, but said there was much more to be done.
"This is a step in the right direction, but it is not a very significant step," said Alexei Ulukayev, an economist at the Institute for the Economy in Transition.
Gazprom, the world's biggest gas producer, is planning to cut 100,000 jobs, or 26 percent of the workforce.
Norilsk Nickel, a major non-ferrous and precious metals producer, said it would shed 10,000 people, or eight percent of its workforce. The workers had asked to leave and would not be replaced.
But economists suggested the reductions might be skin deep and asked whether other companies would follow suit.

"It would be interesting to ask Gazprom what kind of jobs those workers are in -- whether it is direct production or non-core enterprises," said Alexei Kokin, an oil and gas analyst at Renaissance Capital.
"It's not clear to me whether they will be laid off or whether we are talking about purely organisational changes."
But economists said companies which have borne the costs of running entire industrial towns for years could not immediately reap the benefits of a lighter workforce.

Trade union officials at Norilsk, built in 1935 on an Arctic labour camp, estimate that the costs of resettlement and benefit payments would total seven trillion roubles ($1.2 billion), although this is much less than the long term costs of keeping the workers on.

Real layoffs could also summon up one of the great spectres of Russian politics -- unemployment, already 9.6 percent in March under International Labour Organisation methods. But the figures take little account of those who are underemployed or workers who have not been paid for months.

Over-staffed Russian enterprises, who traditionally looked after nursery schools, housing and hospitals as well as production, have generally been slow to jettison the Soviet job-for-life ethos and throw workers into a harsh market.
The government has only recently begun enforcing bankruptcy laws and closing deadbeat companies down.
But economists say harsh measures are inevitable sooner or later if these giant companies are ever to be profitable and the economy is to grow.
"Norilsk Kombinat has 120,000 workers -- it needs about 60,000 to be efficient," said James Fenkner, director of research at CentreInvest Securities.

He quoted figures showing that maintenance of workers and their families in the Arctic circle cost about $2,000 a year per person whereas it would cost $4,000 per person to resettle them elsewhere in Russia.
"The one-off cost as compared to the long-term maintenance costs for unneeded workers has got to be the right choice in the end," Fenkner said.
Other analysts expressed doubt that layoffs were cause for worry over galloping unemployment.
"This is a gradual and long progress, a very slow one," said Renaissance's Kokin, who said restructuring was not just about cutting jobs.
"There are companies that are thinking of cutting jobs, but it will take the form of transferring social responsibilities like kindergartens and hospitals to the city."
